topics.title: Tu or o senhor? How formal to be in Portugal
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about how people address each other in Portugal. This is habit, not law: it varies by region, age, workplace and person, so listen to how others speak to you.
topics.intro: In Portugal you use tu with friends, family, children and people of your own age, and o senhor or a senhora with older strangers and in offices. The word você exists too, but many people in Portugal hear it as cold or a little rude, so it is safer to avoid it at first.
topics.question: Na tua língua há uma forma formal de dizer you? (Does your language have a formal way to say you?)
facts: Use tu with friends, family, children and young people. The verb ends in -s: Como estás? Tens tempo?
Use o senhor with an older man and a senhora with an older woman you do not know, and at the bank, the Junta or Finanças. The verb is in the third person: Como está o senhor?
Often people leave the pronoun out and only use the third-person verb: Quer um café? Precisa de ajuda? This is polite and very common.

Você is in the grammar books, but in Portugal many people find it cold or impolite when you say it to their face. Use o senhor, a senhora or the person's name instead. In Brazil, você is the normal everyday word.
For a group, say vocês, both for friends and in formal situations: Vocês vêm à festa?
Not sure? Start with o senhor or a senhora and wait. Often the other person says: Pode tratar-me por tu (You can use tu with me).

topics.title: Greetings: dois beijinhos, a handshake, Bom dia
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about greetings in Portugal. This is common practice, not a rule: it varies by region, age, family and workplace.
topics.intro: In Portugal people greet with a word first, and often with a touch: dois beijinhos (two light kisses on the cheeks) or a handshake. The greeting changes with the time of day: bom dia, boa tarde, boa noite.
topics.question: Como se cumprimentam as pessoas no teu país? (How do people greet each other in your country?)
facts: Bom dia is for the morning, until about lunch. Boa tarde is for the afternoon. Boa noite is for the evening, and you also say it when you leave at night.
Dois beijinhos: one light kiss on each cheek, often just cheek to cheek. It is common between women, and between a man and a woman who know each other or are introduced by friends.
Men usually shake hands. At work, a handshake is normal at a first meeting.
Olá, tudo bem? is a friendly greeting. The usual answer is Tudo bem, e contigo? (with tu) or Tudo bem, e consigo? (polite).
When you enter a small shop, a café or a lift, many people say bom dia or boa tarde to everybody.
Thank you depends on the speaker: a man says obrigado, a woman says obrigada.

topics.title: Daily rhythm: meal times, opening hours, Sundays and feriados
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about daily life in Portugal. Opening hours are set by each business and change by town, season and type of shop, so check the door or the website. As of 2026-11.
topics.intro: In Portugal lunch is usually between about 12:30 and 2 pm, and dinner often starts around 8 pm. Big supermarkets and shopping centres open every day, but small shops in smaller towns may close for lunch and on Sunday.
topics.question: A que horas almoças e jantas no teu país? (At what time do you have lunch and dinner in your country?)
facts: A hora do almoço (lunch time) is important. Many people eat a full hot meal at lunch, often the prato do dia in a café or restaurant.
Dinner (o jantar) often starts at about 8 pm or later. Many restaurants open for dinner around 7 or 7:30 pm.
Shopping centres (centros comerciais) usually open every day, often until late in the evening. Most big supermarkets open on Sundays too.
In smaller towns, some small shops and services close for one or two hours at lunch time. A sign says: Encerrado para almoço.
On public holidays (feriados), many offices, banks and small shops close. Supermarkets and shopping centres often stay open.
There is always a pharmacy open at night and on Sundays: the farmácia de serviço. Every pharmacy shows on its door which one is on duty.

topics.title: Cafés and paying: a bica, a conta and tipping
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about cafés and restaurants in Portugal. Tipping is a habit, not a rule, and it varies. The NIF on the invoice (e-fatura) follows the tax rules of the Autoridade Tributária, which can change; as of 2026-11.
topics.intro: In a Portuguese café you often order at the counter, and a small coffee is very cheap. In a restaurant you ask for a conta (the bill), and a tip is a small extra, not a rule.
topics.question: No teu país deixas gorjeta no café? (Do you leave a tip in a café in your country?)
facts: Um café is a small strong espresso. In Lisbon many people call it uma bica. Um galão is milky coffee in a tall glass, and uma meia de leite is half coffee, half milk in a cup.
With a coffee, many people have a pastry from the pastelaria, for example um pastel de nata.
In a restaurant, bread, olives or butter (o couvert) are often put on the table before you order. If you eat them, they are on the bill. If you do not want them, you can say: Não, obrigado.
To pay, ask: A conta, por favor. In a café you often just ask: Quanto é?
Tipping (a gorjeta) is not required. Many people leave the small change in a café, and some leave about 5 to 10 percent in a restaurant when the service was good.
At the till you often hear: Quer contribuinte? or Com NIF? It means: do you want your tax number on the invoice? You can say yes and give your NIF, or say não.

topics.title: The regions: mainland, Madeira and the Azores
topics.sourceNote: Facts from the Constitution of the Portuguese Republic (autonomous regions), INE (population, NUTS regions) and the regional governments of the Azores and Madeira. Population figures are rounded estimates and change; the NUTS map was revised for 2024. As of 2026-11.
topics.intro: Portugal is made up of the mainland (o continente) and two groups of islands in the Atlantic, the Azores (os Açores) and Madeira, which are autonomous regions. The mainland is divided into 18 distritos, and you will hear the names of the big regions, like the Norte, the Alentejo or the Algarve, every day.
topics.question: De que região do teu país és? (Which region of your country are you from?)
facts: About 10.6 million people live in Portugal. Most live near the coast, especially around Lisboa and Porto, the two big metropolitan areas.
The mainland has 18 distritos, for example Lisboa, Porto, Braga, Coimbra, Faro and Évora. Today they matter mostly as names and as the constituencies for the national elections.
For statistics and EU funds Portugal uses NUTS regions. On the mainland you will hear Norte, Centro, the Lisbon area, Alentejo and Algarve.

The Azores (os Açores) are nine islands in the middle of the Atlantic, for example São Miguel, Terceira, Pico and Faial. The regional government's president sits in Ponta Delgada and the regional parliament in Horta.
Madeira is an archipelago with two inhabited islands, Madeira and Porto Santo. Its capital is Funchal.
The Azores and Madeira are autonomous regions (regiões autónomas). They have their own regional parliament and government, but they are part of Portugal, which is not a federal state.

topics.title: Public holidays: national, municipal and regional
topics.sourceNote: National holidays as set in the Código do Trabalho (article 234) after the four holidays suspended in 2013 were restored in 2016. Municipal holidays are set by each câmara municipal; regional holidays by the Azores and Madeira. Carnaval is not a mandatory holiday. As of 2026-11.
topics.intro: Portugal has 13 national public holidays (feriados nacionais), and every município adds one municipal holiday of its own. On a feriado many offices, schools, banks and small shops are closed.
topics.question: Qual é o feriado mais importante no teu país? (What is the most important public holiday in your country?)
facts: Some holidays are about history: 25 de Abril (Freedom Day, the 1974 revolution), 5 de Outubro (the Republic, 1910) and 1 de Dezembro (independence restored in 1640).
10 de Junho is the Dia de Portugal, de Camões e das Comunidades Portuguesas, the national day, which also celebrates the Portuguese who live abroad.
Several holidays are religious: Sexta-feira Santa (Good Friday), Páscoa (Easter), Corpo de Deus, 15 de Agosto, 1 de Novembro (All Saints), 8 de Dezembro and Natal (25 December).
Each município has a feriado municipal. Lisboa celebrates Santo António on 13 June and Porto celebrates São João on 24 June.
The autonomous regions have their own day: Madeira on 1 July, and the Azores on the Monday after Pentecost (Segunda-feira do Espírito Santo).

Carnaval (Tuesday before Lent) is not a national holiday, but many schools and public offices close. When a holiday falls on a Tuesday or Thursday, some people take the day in between off: fazer ponte.

topics.title: Food and meals: pequeno-almoço, prato do dia, bacalhau
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about food in Portugal. Dishes and habits vary by region and family; the dishes named here are widely known and documented in regional cookbooks and tourism sources of the regions.
topics.intro: Meals in Portugal have their own names: o pequeno-almoço, o almoço, o lanche and o jantar. Lunch is often a full hot meal with soup, a main dish and coffee.
topics.question: Qual é o prato típico da tua região? (What is the typical dish of your region?)
facts: Breakfast (o pequeno-almoço) is often small: a coffee, bread or toast, or a pastry. O lanche is a snack in the afternoon.
Many cafés and restaurants offer a prato do dia (dish of the day) at lunch. Often a meal starts with soup (a sopa), for example caldo verde, made with potatoes and thin strips of cabbage.
Bacalhau (dried salted cod) is the best-known ingredient. It is soaked in water before cooking and is prepared in many ways, for example bacalhau à Brás or bacalhau com natas.

Some regional dishes: francesinha (a big meat sandwich with sauce) in Porto, cozido à portuguesa (meat and vegetables), arroz de marisco (seafood rice), and grilled sardines (sardinhas assadas) in June.

In Madeira you will find espetada (beef on a skewer, traditionally of laurel wood) and bolo do caco (a flat bread with garlic butter). In the Azores, on São Miguel, cozido das Furnas is cooked in the hot volcanic ground, and São Jorge is known for its cheese.
Before a meal people say Bom apetite! In the Portuguese of Portugal, a sobremesa is the dessert.

topics.title: Festas populares: Santo António, São João and the year's festivals
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about festivals in Portugal, as described by the town halls and regional tourism boards. Dates of local festas change from year to year, so check the câmara municipal or junta de freguesia. As of 2026-11.
topics.intro: In June, many Portuguese towns celebrate the Santos Populares (the popular saints) with music, grilled sardines and street parties. All through the year, towns and villages have their own festas and romarias.
topics.question: Qual é a festa mais bonita da tua cidade? (What is the most beautiful festival in your town?)
facts: Santo António is the big festa in Lisboa, on the night of 12 to 13 June. The neighbourhoods march down the Avenida da Liberdade (the marchas populares), and people give each other a small basil plant, o manjerico.
São João is the big festa in Porto, on the night of 23 to 24 June. People walk through the streets until morning and hit each other lightly on the head with soft plastic hammers.
In summer, many towns and villages, especially in the north, have a romaria: a religious procession together with a fair, music and food.
Carnaval is in February or March. Some towns, such as Torres Vedras, Ovar and Loulé, are known for their parades.

At Christmas the main meal is often a consoada on the evening of 24 December, often with bacalhau and boiled vegetables, and a bolo-rei (king cake). At Easter, many families eat folar and amêndoas (sugared almonds).

In the Azores, the Festas do Espírito Santo are held in spring and summer, with shared meals such as the sopas do Espírito Santo. Madeira is known for its Festa da Flor in spring and for its New Year's Eve fireworks.

topics.title: Fado and music in Portugal
topics.sourceNote: Facts from the UNESCO lists of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (fado 2011, cante alentejano 2014) and the Museu do Fado in Lisbon. Customs in casas de fado vary from house to house.
topics.intro: Fado is a song style from Portugal, sung by one voice with the guitarra portuguesa and a classical guitar. Since 2011 it has been on the UNESCO list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
topics.question: Que música é típica do teu país? (What music is typical of your country?)
facts: Fado grew up in the old neighbourhoods of Lisboa, such as Alfama and Mouraria, in the 19th century. Its songs often talk about love, the sea, the city and saudade, a feeling of missing someone or something.
The guitarra portuguesa is a pear-shaped guitar with twelve strings. It plays together with the viola, which in Portugal means the classical guitar.
There is also fado de Coimbra, linked to the university. It is traditionally sung by men, often students in black capes.
In a casa de fados (a fado restaurant), people stop talking while someone sings. You may hear: Silêncio, que se vai cantar o fado.
Amália Rodrigues (1920–1999) is the most famous fado singer. Today many singers, such as Mariza, Carminho and Camané, are known abroad too.
Fado is not the only tradition. Cante alentejano, a group singing without instruments from the Alentejo, has been on the UNESCO list since 2014.

topics.title: Recycling: the ecopontos
topics.sourceNote: The colours of the ecopontos are used across Portugal (Sociedade Ponto Verde, the municipal waste services). What goes in which container, and the collection of food waste and bulky items, is decided by each município, so check your câmara's website. As of 2026-11.
topics.intro: In Portugal you sort your rubbish into the ecoponto, a group of coloured containers in the street. Blue is for paper, yellow for packaging and green for glass.
topics.question: No teu país separas o lixo? (Do you sort your rubbish in your country?)
facts: The ecopontos are usually in the street, not in your building. You take your sorted rubbish there.
Azul (blue): paper and cardboard, for example newspapers and flattened boxes (o papelão).
Amarelo (yellow): plastic and metal packaging, for example bottles, yogurt pots, tins and drink cartons.
Verde (green): glass bottles and jars, without lids. Many people call this container o vidrão. Plates, mirrors and light bulbs do not go here.
Everything else goes into the normal bin for general waste (o lixo indiferenciado). Many towns now also collect food waste (os biorresíduos) separately, often in a brown container.
Batteries go into the small pilhão and used cooking oil into the oleão. For old furniture (os monos), call the câmara municipal or the junta: many towns collect them for free on a set day.

topics.intro: At many public offices in Portugal you are served by number: you take a senha (a ticket) and wait until it is called. For more and more services you need a marcação (an appointment) booked online or by phone first.
topics.question: No teu país tens de marcar hora para ir às finanças? (In your country, do you need an appointment for the tax office?)

Many offices work com marcação (with an appointment) or have fewer places sem marcação (without one). Check before you go.
A Loja do Cidadão is a building with many public services in one place, for example Finanças, Segurança Social and the Cartão de Cidadão desk. A smaller Espaço Cidadão is often in a junta or câmara.
Many services are online on gov.pt or on the office's own portal. To log in you can use the Chave Móvel Digital, a digital key linked to your phone number.
AIMA, the agency for immigration, usually gives appointments itself, by its online portal, by email or by phone. The rules change often, so always check AIMA's website.
By law, some people get atendimento prioritário (served first): for example people with a disability, pregnant women, people with a small child and older people.

topics.title: Your first numbers: NIF, NISS, número de utente and the atestado
topics.sourceNote: General orientation from the public portals: gov.pt (ePortugal), portaldasfinancas.gov.pt (Autoridade Tributária), seg-social.pt (Segurança Social), sns.gov.pt (SNS) and aima.gov.pt (AIMA), as of 2026-11. What each office asks for can change and can differ between offices, so check the official page before you go. This is general orientation, not legal advice.
topics.intro: When you start a life in Portugal, you collect a few numbers and papers that almost every office, employer and landlord will ask for. The most important are the NIF (tax number), the NISS (social security number), the número de utente (health service number) and, often, an atestado de residência from your Junta de Freguesia.
topics.question: Que documentos precisaste quando chegaste a Portugal? (Which documents did you need when you arrived in Portugal?)
facts: The NIF (número de identificação fiscal), also called número de contribuinte, is your tax number. You get it from the Finanças (Autoridade Tributária) at a tax office, a Loja do Cidadão or, in some cases, online. You need it to rent a flat, sign a work contract, open a bank account and even for a phone contract.
The NISS (número de identificação da Segurança Social) is your social security number. You ask for it at the Segurança Social, and an employer needs it to register you and pay contributions.
The número de utente is your number in the public health service (SNS). You usually ask for it at the centro de saúde of the area where you live.

The atestado de residência is a certificate from your Junta de Freguesia (the parish council) that says you live at an address. Offices often ask for it as proof of address. What the Junta asks for varies: for example an ID, a document with your address, or the signature of witnesses who live in the freguesia.
Citizens of the EU, the EEA and Switzerland who stay more than three months register at the Câmara Municipal (town hall) and receive a certificado de registo de cidadão da UE (CRUE).

Citizens of other countries need a visa or an autorização de residência (residence permit). This is handled by AIMA (Agência para a Integração, Migrações e Asilo), which replaced the SEF in 2023. The rules have changed several times since 2024, so check aima.gov.pt.

topics.title: Public health: SNS, centro de saúde, SNS 24 and urgências
topics.sourceNote: From sns.gov.pt, sns24.gov.pt and the Lei de Bases da Saúde (Lei 95/2019, dre.pt), as of 2026-11. Rules on registration, family doctors and fees are changed from time to time and are applied differently between regions and health centres. This is general orientation, not medical or legal advice.
topics.intro: Portugal has a national health service, the Serviço Nacional de Saúde (SNS), which is paid for mainly through taxes. Your first door is the centro de saúde of the area where you live, and for advice at any hour there is the SNS 24 phone line.
topics.question: No teu país, onde vais primeiro quando estás doente? (In your country, where do you go first when you are ill?)
facts: To use the SNS you register at the centro de saúde of your area and get a número de utente. In many places the centro de saúde is called a USF (Unidade de Saúde Familiar).
In principle each person has a médico de família (family doctor). In some regions many people still have no family doctor, so ask at your centro de saúde what to do in that case.
SNS 24 (808 24 24 24, or sns24.gov.pt) gives advice by phone at any hour. A nurse asks questions and tells you where to go: self-care, the centro de saúde or the hospital.
For a real emergency, call 112. The urgências (A&E) of a hospital are for serious cases. If you can, call SNS 24 first, because it can refer you.
Most taxas moderadoras (small user fees) were abolished between 2020 and 2022. A fee can still be charged in hospital urgências if you go without a referral and are not admitted.
The farmácia (pharmacy) is often the first stop for small problems. A pharmacist can give advice, and many medicines need a receita (prescription), which usually arrives as a code on your phone.

topics.title: Renting a flat: contrato, renda, caução and condomínio
topics.sourceNote: From the Novo Regime do Arrendamento Urbano and the Código Civil (dre.pt), the Portal das Finanças (rent receipts and contract registration) and gov.pt, as of 2026-11. Housing law in Portugal was changed several times in recent years (for example the Mais Habitação package of 2023). This is general orientation, not legal advice: read your contract and ask a lawyer or a tenants' association if in doubt.
topics.intro: In Portugal a rental is based on a written contrato de arrendamento between you and the senhorio or senhoria (landlord). Flats are described by their number of bedrooms: a T1 has one bedroom, a T2 two, and a T0 is a studio.
topics.question: No teu país, quanto se paga normalmente de caução? (In your country, how much deposit do people usually pay?)
facts: The contrato de arrendamento should be written and signed by both sides. It states the renda (monthly rent), the duration, the date of payment and who pays which costs.
Landlords usually ask for a caução (deposit), often one or two months' rent, and sometimes rent in advance. Some also ask for a fiador (guarantor), a person who pays if you do not.
The landlord must register the contract with the Finanças. This matters to you: a registered contract helps as proof of address and for some benefits and tax deductions.
For each payment you should get a recibo de renda eletrónico (electronic rent receipt), which most landlords issue on the Portal das Finanças. Keep it: rent can count for your IRS (income tax).
In a block of flats the owners form a condomínio, which pays for cleaning, the lift and repairs of shared parts. Usually the owner pays the quota do condomínio, but check your contract.
Water, electricity, gas and internet are often in the tenant's name. You sign the contracts with the suppliers and need your NIF.

topics.title: The school system: pré-escolar, ensino básico, secundário
topics.sourceNote: From the Lei de Bases do Sistema Educativo and Lei 85/2009 on compulsory schooling (dre.pt), gov.pt and the Portal das Matrículas, as of 2026-11. Dates for enrolment and exams change every school year; check the current calendar.
topics.intro: In Portugal school is compulsory from the age of 6 until 18, or until the student finishes the 12.º ano (year 12). Public schools are free, and most of them are organised in agrupamentos de escolas (groups of schools) under one management.
topics.question: Com que idade começam as crianças a escola no teu país? (At what age do children start school in your country?)
facts: The pré-escolar (pre-school, in a jardim de infância) is for children from 3 to 5. It is not compulsory, but most children go.
The ensino básico lasts nine years and has three stages: the 1.º ciclo (years 1 to 4), the 2.º ciclo (years 5 and 6) and the 3.º ciclo (years 7 to 9).
The ensino secundário covers years 10 to 12. Students choose a general course that prepares for university, or a curso profissional (vocational course) that also gives a professional qualification.
Exames nacionais (national exams) take place at the end of some years of the secundário. Their results count for the final grade and for entry to university.
You enrol your child (fazer a matrícula) online on the Portal das Matrículas or at the school. Children who arrive from abroad can enrol during the year too.
Pupils whose first language is not Portuguese can have classes of Português Língua Não Materna (PLNM) at school. Ask the school about it at enrolment.

topics.title: Finding a job: IEFP, currículo and contract types
topics.sourceNote: From the Código do Trabalho (dre.pt), iefp.pt and gov.pt, as of 2026-11. The minimum wage is set every year by the Government, and labour rules were changed by the Agenda do Trabalho Digno (2023). This is general orientation, not legal advice; check your contract and the current law.
topics.intro: In Portugal people find work through job websites, personal contacts and the public employment service, the IEFP (Instituto do Emprego e Formação Profissional). Before you start, make sure you have your NIF and NISS, because the employer needs them.
topics.question: Como encontraste o teu último trabalho? (How did you find your last job?)
facts: The IEFP runs the centros de emprego (job centres). You can register there, look at job offers on iefp.pt and ask about training courses, including Portuguese courses for foreigners.
A currículo (CV) is usually one or two pages. Many people send it with a short carta de apresentação (cover letter) by e-mail or through a job website.
A contrato sem termo is a permanent contract. A contrato a termo certo ends on a fixed date, and a contrato a termo incerto ends when a task ends, for example when a colleague comes back from leave.
Most contracts start with a período experimental (trial period), in general 90 days for a permanent contract. During this time either side can end the contract more easily.
Salaries are usually paid in 14 payments a year: 12 monthly salaries plus the subsídio de férias (holiday pay) and the subsídio de Natal (Christmas pay).

Self-employed people often work with recibos verdes (green receipts), invoices issued on the Portal das Finanças. The salário mínimo nacional (national minimum wage) is set every year; for 2026 it was set at 920 euros a month.

topics.intro: Portuguese is the official language of Portugal and the first language of almost everyone who grows up there. Two more languages have legal recognition: Mirandese, spoken around Miranda do Douro, and Portuguese Sign Language.

Mirandese (o mirandês) is a language of its own, not a dialect of Portuguese. It is spoken in the area of Miranda do Douro, in the north-east, close to Spain. A law of 1999 (Lei 7/99) recognised the right to learn and use it there.
Língua Gestual Portuguesa (LGP), Portuguese Sign Language, is protected by the Constitution since 1997. It is different from the sign languages of other countries.
Portuguese is pluricentric: Portugal, Brazil and the African countries each have their own standard. This course teaches European Portuguese, the standard of Portugal.
Accents differ inside Portugal too. In the north many people pronounce v like b, Lisbon speakers reduce unstressed vowels a lot, and the Azores (especially São Miguel) have a very distinct accent.

Since the 1990 Orthographic Agreement, Portugal writes many words without silent consonants: ação instead of acção, ótimo instead of óptimo. You will still see the old spelling on older signs and in older books.

topics.intro: Portuguese is an official language in nine countries on four continents, and most of its speakers live in Brazil. This course teaches the Portuguese of Portugal, but you will hear Brazilian and African Portuguese too, so it helps to know the main differences.
topics.question: Que língua se fala no teu país, e há muitas maneiras de a falar? (Which language is spoken in your country, and are there many ways to speak it?)
facts: Portuguese is official in Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé e Príncipe, Timor-Leste and Equatorial Guinea. In Macau (China) it is co-official with Chinese.
These nine countries form the CPLP, the Comunidade dos Países de Língua Portuguesa, founded in Lisbon in 1996. The 5th of May is the Dia Mundial da Língua Portuguesa.
Well over 250 million people speak Portuguese, and most of them live in Brazil. That is why many apps, films and online videos use Brazilian Portuguese.

European Portuguese sounds very different from Brazilian Portuguese: in Portugal unstressed vowels are often swallowed, so telefone can sound like “tlfon”. Brazilian speakers pronounce the vowels more fully.

Grammar differs too. In Portugal people say estou a trabalhar (I am working), and in Brazil estou trabalhando. In Portugal você can sound distant and people prefer tu or o senhor / a senhora; in Brazil você is the normal word for you.

Many everyday words differ: Portugal says o comboio, o autocarro, o telemóvel and o pequeno-almoço, and Brazil says o trem, o ônibus, o celular and o café da manhã. In Angola, Mozambique and the other countries, the written standard is close to Portugal's, with words from local languages. The 1990 Orthographic Agreement brought the spelling closer, but some differences remain (facto in Portugal, fato in Brazil).

topics.title: Training and university: licenciatura, CTeSP and recognising your degree
topics.sourceNote: From dges.gov.pt (Direção-Geral do Ensino Superior: access to higher education and recognition of foreign degrees, Decreto-Lei 66/2018), iefp.pt and gov.pt, as of 2026-11. Fees, deadlines and the documents asked for change; the official pages are right if they differ from this one.
topics.intro: After secondary school, Portugal offers two kinds of higher education, universidades and institutos politécnicos, as well as vocational training. If you studied abroad, your degree can be recognised through the DGES or a higher education institution.
topics.question: O teu diploma é reconhecido em Portugal? (Is your degree recognised in Portugal?)
facts: Higher education follows the Bologna system: a licenciatura (bachelor's degree) usually lasts three years, a mestrado (master's) one and a half to two years, and a doutoramento (doctorate) about three to four years. Some fields, such as medicine, have a mestrado integrado.
Universidades focus more on research and theory, institutos politécnicos more on practice. Politécnicos also offer CTeSP (Cursos Técnicos Superiores Profissionais), two-year practical courses.

Most students enter public higher education through the Concurso Nacional de Acesso, organised by the DGES, using their school grades and exam results. There are also special routes, for example for international students and for people over 23.
Students pay propinas (tuition fees). For public licenciaturas there is a legal maximum; private institutions set their own fees.

Foreign higher education degrees can be recognised in three ways: reconhecimento automático (for degrees on an approved list), de nível (the level is recognised) and específico (compared with a specific Portuguese degree). Some regulated professions, such as doctors, nurses and engineers, also need the professional body (Ordem) to accept you.

Secondary school certificates from abroad are made equivalent (equivalência) through a school or the education services. Vocational training for adults is offered by the IEFP and many training centres.

topics.title: Leaving a job: aviso prévio, despedimento and subsídio de desemprego
topics.sourceNote: From the Código do Trabalho (dre.pt), seg-social.pt (subsídio de desemprego) and iefp.pt, as of 2026-11. Labour law has many special cases (contract type, seniority, collective agreements), and the rules on benefits change. This is general orientation, not legal advice: for your own case ask the ACT (Autoridade para as Condições do Trabalho), a union or a lawyer.
topics.intro: How a job ends in Portugal decides what you are owed and whether you can get unemployment benefit. The main ways are your own notice (denúncia), a dismissal by the employer (despedimento) and an agreement between both sides (revogação por mútuo acordo).
topics.question: No teu país, com quanto tempo de antecedência tens de avisar quando te despedes? (In your country, how much notice do you have to give when you quit?)
facts: If you want to leave a permanent contract, you send a written denúncia with aviso prévio (notice). In general it is 30 days if you have worked there up to two years and 60 days if longer. Your contract or collective agreement can say something different.

The employer cannot dismiss you without a reason. The Constitution forbids dismissal sem justa causa, and the law lists the possible grounds and procedures, for example serious misconduct or a collective dismissal.

With a revogação por mútuo acordo, you and the employer agree in writing to end the contract, often with a sum of money. Read it carefully before you sign, because it can affect your right to unemployment benefit.

At the end you are paid what you are owed: salary for the days worked, holidays not taken and the proportional part of the subsídio de férias and de Natal. In some cases there is also a compensação (severance pay).
The employer must give you a certificado de trabalho and, if you lose the job involuntarily, a declaração de situação de desemprego for the Segurança Social.

The subsídio de desemprego is for people who lose their job involuntarily and have paid enough contributions. You must register at the centro de emprego (IEFP) and apply to the Segurança Social within a set deadline.

topics.intro: RTP (Rádio e Televisão de Portugal) is Portugal's public broadcaster, with television channels, radio stations and a free online platform. It is paid for mainly by the contribuição audiovisual, a small monthly charge on the electricity bill, plus some advertising.
topics.question: No teu país, quem paga a televisão pública? (In your country, who pays for public television?)
facts: RTP runs national TV channels such as RTP1, RTP2 and the news channel RTP3, regional channels for the Azores and Madeira (RTP Açores, RTP Madeira) and channels abroad (RTP Internacional, RTP África).
Its radio stations include Antena 1 (news, talk and Portuguese music), Antena 2 (classical music and culture) and Antena 3 (pop and youth). RTP Play streams most programmes for free.
The contribuição audiovisual is charged on most household electricity bills. You do not register a TV set: you pay through the electricity contract.
RTP1 carries some advertising, but with stricter limits than private channels. The main private channels are SIC and TVI.
The ERC is the independent regulator of the media. It supervises pluralism and the rules for all broadcasters, public and private.
Lusa is the national news agency, mostly owned by the state. Many newspapers, radios and websites use its news.

topics.intro: The Portuguese-speaking countries share a language, but each has its own music, festivals and food. In Portugal you will meet many people from Brazil, Cabo Verde, Angola and Mozambique, and knowing a few of their traditions makes conversations easier.
topics.question: Que festa ou prato do teu país gostarias de mostrar a um amigo? (Which festival or dish from your country would you like to show a friend?)
facts: Brazil: o Carnaval takes place in the days before Lent. In Rio de Janeiro the escolas de samba parade in the Sambódromo, and in Salvador and Recife/Olinda people dance in the streets behind music trucks and bands, to axé and frevo.

Brazil: as festas juninas are held in June, above all in the Northeast. People dance the quadrilha, wear country costumes and eat dishes made from milho (maize). A typical Brazilian dish is a feijoada, black beans cooked with several kinds of pork.

Cabo Verde: a morna is a slow, melancholic song, often compared with fado. It has been on the UNESCO list of Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2019, and Cesária Évora made it known around the world. The national dish is a cachupa, a stew of maize, beans and fish or meat.

Angola: semba is a popular dance music, and kizomba grew out of it in Angola in the 1980s. Today kizomba is danced in many countries, including in dance schools in Lisbon. A well-known dish is a muamba de galinha, chicken in palm oil, often eaten with funge.
Mozambique: a marrabenta is a dance music that grew up in and around Maputo in the 20th century. Mozambican cooking uses a lot of coconut, seafood and piri-piri.

In Portugal, especially around Lisbon, you can find these traditions in restaurants, concerts and festivals run by the communities from these countries. Asking someone about the music or food of their country is a friendly way to start a conversation.

topics.title: State and local power: Republic, municípios, freguesias and the autonomous regions
topics.sourceNote: Based on the Constituição da República Portuguesa (parlamento.pt) and the official sites of the Presidência (presidencia.pt) and the Governo (portugal.gov.pt), as of 2026-11. The number of freguesias changed with the reforms of 2013 and 2025, so this page gives no exact figure. General orientation, not legal advice.
topics.intro: Portugal is a unitary state, not a federation: laws for the whole country are made in Lisbon, and only the Azores and Madeira have their own regional parliaments and governments. For daily life, the levels you deal with most are the município (with its Câmara Municipal) and the freguesia (with its Junta de Freguesia).
topics.question: No teu país, quem decide sobre as escolas, as estradas e o lixo? (In your country, who decides about schools, roads and rubbish?)
facts: The Constitution names four órgãos de soberania: the Presidente da República, the Assembleia da República (parliament), the Governo, led by the Primeiro-Ministro, and the courts (os tribunais).

Portugal has 308 municípios (concelhos). Each has a Câmara Municipal, the executive led by the presidente da câmara, and an Assembleia Municipal that debates and votes. The câmara deals with things like local roads, rubbish collection, urban planning and some social services.

Each município is divided into freguesias, a little over three thousand in total. The Junta de Freguesia is the closest level of administration: it issues the atestado de residência and runs local services. The number of freguesias was cut sharply in 2013, and some were restored in 2025.

The Azores (Açores) and Madeira are autonomous regions. Each has its own Assembleia Legislativa and Governo Regional, which make laws and decisions on regional matters. A Representante da República represents the State in each region.

On the mainland there are no elected regions. The Constitution allows them, but a proposal to create them was rejected in a referendum in 1998. Instead, five CCDRs (Comissões de Coordenação e Desenvolvimento Regional) plan regional development, and the municípios work together in comunidades intermunicipais and in the áreas metropolitanas of Lisbon and Porto.
The 18 distritos of the mainland are an old division. They matter today mainly as electoral constituencies and in the names of some services, not as a level of government.

topics.title: Segurança Social: NISS, contributions and benefits
topics.sourceNote: Based on the official site of the Segurança Social (seg-social.pt) and the Guia Prático leaflets published there, as of 2026-11. Contribution rates, the retirement age and the conditions for benefits change; the figures here are the general regime and must be checked for your case. General orientation, not legal advice.
topics.intro: The Segurança Social is the public system that pays pensions, sick pay, parental pay, unemployment benefit and family allowances. You need a NISS (número de identificação da Segurança Social) as soon as you work in Portugal, whether you are employed or self-employed.
topics.question: No teu país, quem paga quando estás doente e não podes trabalhar? (In your country, who pays when you are ill and cannot work?)
facts: The NISS is your Segurança Social number. Employers need it to register you, and you need it to receive any benefit. You can ask for it at a Segurança Social office or online, and employers can request it for a new worker.

Employees and employers pay contributions every month, the Taxa Social Única (TSU). In the general regime the worker pays 11 % of the gross salary and the employer about 23 % on top. The employer deducts your part from your pay.

Self-employed workers (trabalhadores independentes, often paid with recibos verdes) declare their income every three months and pay contributions themselves. New self-employed workers are usually exempt for the first year.

Segurança Social Direta is the online service. There you can see your contributions, ask for documents, update your bank details (IBAN) and apply for many benefits. To log in you use a password or the Chave Móvel Digital.

The legal retirement age (idade normal de acesso à pensão de velhice) is linked to life expectancy and is set again every year. It is now a little over 66. Your pension depends on how many years you contributed and on your earnings.

Benefits include subsídio de doença (sick pay, with a baixa from a doctor), subsídio parental (parental pay), subsídio de desemprego (unemployment benefit, see Leaving a job) and abono de família (child allowance). Each has its own conditions, such as a minimum period of contributions.

topics.title: Elections and the electoral system
topics.sourceNote: Based on the Constitution, the electoral laws and the information of the Comissão Nacional de Eleições (cne.pt) and the Assembleia da República (parlamento.pt), as of 2026-11. Who may vote as a foreign resident depends on nationality, residence and reciprocity agreements, and the details change; check with the CNE or your Junta de Freguesia. topics.intro: In Portugal you vote for party lists in parliamentary elections and directly for a person in presidential elections. Voting is a right, not an obligation, and foreign residents can vote in some elections, depending on their nationality.
topics.question: No teu país, votar é obrigatório? (In your country, is voting compulsory?)
facts: The Assembleia da República has 230 deputados, elected for four years. Seats are shared out with the D'Hondt method in electoral constituencies (círculos eleitorais): one for each mainland distrito, one each for the Azores and Madeira, and two for Portuguese citizens living abroad (Europa and Fora da Europa).

After an election, the Presidente da República appoints the Primeiro-Ministro, taking into account the results. The Governo needs the support, or at least the tolerance, of parliament to stay in office.

The Presidente da República is elected directly for five years. A candidate needs more than half of the valid votes; if no one gets that, the two leading candidates meet in a second round. A president can serve at most two terms in a row.

There are also elections for the municípios and freguesias (eleições autárquicas, every four years), for the European Parliament (every five years) and for the regional parliaments of the Azores and Madeira.
Portuguese citizens from 18 are registered to vote automatically. Elections are held on a Sunday, and the day before is a dia de reflexão, when campaigning is not allowed.

Foreign residents: citizens of other EU countries can vote in local and European elections if they register. Citizens of some other countries, such as Brazil and Cabo Verde, can vote in local elections under reciprocity rules after some years of legal residence. Brazilian citizens with the estatuto de igualdade de direitos políticos can vote in more elections. Check the current conditions before you register.

topics.title: Portugal and the Portuguese-speaking world: a shared history
topics.sourceNote: General historical overview written neutrally. Dates are standard in history reference works; figures on migration follow the official reports of the Portuguese migration authorities, as of 2026-11. Historians, governments and communities in the different countries assess these events differently, and this page does not take a side.
topics.intro: Portugal and the other Portuguese-speaking countries share more than five centuries of history, from the sea voyages of the 15th century to the independence of the African colonies in the 1970s. The same events are remembered very differently in Lisbon, Luanda, Maputo or Rio de Janeiro, and they still shape migration and friendships today.
topics.question: Como se ensina a história colonial no teu país? (How is colonial history taught in your country?)
facts: In the 15th and 16th centuries Portuguese ships explored the coast of Africa and reached India (Vasco da Gama, 1498) and Brazil (Pedro Álvares Cabral, 1500). Portugal built an empire of trading posts and colonies in Africa, Asia and South America. In Portugal this period is often called os Descobrimentos, a term that is debated today.

The empire was built on violence and forced labour. Portugal was one of the largest carriers in the Atlantic slave trade: millions of Africans were taken by force, many of them to Brazil. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.
Brazil became independent on 7 September 1822, declared by Pedro, the son of the Portuguese king, who became Emperor of Brazil.

From 1961 to 1974 Portugal fought colonial wars against independence movements in Angola, Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique. After the revolution of 25 April 1974, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cabo Verde, São Tomé e Príncipe and Angola became independent in 1974–1975. Hundreds of thousands of Portuguese settlers, the retornados, came back to Portugal.

Timor-Leste declared independence in 1975 and was occupied by Indonesia days later. After a referendum in 1999 and a period under UN administration, it became independent in 2002. Macau was handed over to China in 1999.

Today the countries cooperate in the CPLP, founded in 1996, and people move in all directions: many Portuguese emigrated to Brazil and Africa in the past, and today people from Brazil, Cabo Verde, Angola, Guinea-Bissau and the other countries are among the largest groups of foreign residents in Portugal. How to remember the colonial past, in museums, monuments and schools, is discussed openly in Portugal.

topics.title: 25 April 1974: the Carnation Revolution and the end of the dictatorship
topics.sourceNote: General historical overview written neutrally, based on history reference works and the materials of the Assembleia da República (parlamento.pt) and the Centro de Documentação 25 de Abril. Dates are standard; figures such as turnout are rounded. How the revolution and the period after it are judged differs between people and parties, and this page does not take a side.
topics.intro: On 25 April 1974 a military coup ended almost fifty years of dictatorship in Portugal, and the day became known as the Revolução dos Cravos (Carnation Revolution). It led to democracy, to the Constitution of 1976 and to the independence of the African colonies, and 25 April is a national holiday, the Dia da Liberdade.
topics.question: Há no teu país uma data que se lembra como o início da liberdade? (Is there a date in your country that is remembered as the beginning of freedom?)
facts: After a military coup in 1926, Portugal was ruled by a dictatorship. From 1933 it was called the Estado Novo, led by António de Oliveira Salazar and, from 1968, by Marcelo Caetano. There were no free elections, the press was censored, and the political police (PIDE) persecuted opponents.
From 1961 the regime fought colonial wars in Angola, Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique. Many young men were conscripted and many others emigrated, often to France, to avoid the war or poverty.

On 25 April 1974 a group of officers, the Movimento das Forças Armadas (MFA), took power almost without fighting. Two songs on the radio were the signals for the operation, the second being Grândola, Vila Morena by José (Zeca) Afonso. People came into the streets and put red carnations into the soldiers' rifles.

The period that followed, the PREC (Processo Revolucionário em Curso), was full of conflict: banks and large companies were nationalised, land was occupied in the Alentejo, and political camps fought over the direction of the country. A military confrontation on 25 November 1975 is generally seen as the end of this period.
On 25 April 1975 Portugal held its first free elections with universal suffrage, for the Assembleia Constituinte, with a very high turnout of over 90 %. The new Constitution was approved in 1976.

Today 25 April is a public holiday with ceremonies in parliament and parades with carnations. In 2024 Portugal marked 50 years of the revolution. People still debate how to remember the Estado Novo, the colonial wars and the PREC.

topics.title: The Constitution of 1976 and the Constitutional Court
topics.sourceNote: Based on the text of the Constituição da República Portuguesa (parlamento.pt) and the information of the Tribunal Constitucional (tribunalconstitucional.pt) and the Provedor de Justiça (provedor-jus.pt), as of 2026-11. General orientation, not legal advice.
topics.intro: The Constituição da República Portuguesa was approved on 2 April 1976 and came into force on 25 April 1976, two years after the revolution. It is the highest law of the country, and the Tribunal Constitucional checks that other laws respect it.
topics.question: Conheces algum direito que a Constituição do teu país garante? (Do you know a right that your country's Constitution guarantees?)
facts: The Constitution was written by the Assembleia Constituinte elected on 25 April 1975. It sets out the órgãos de soberania, the rights of citizens and the organisation of the economy and of local power.

It has been revised seven times. The revision of 1982 ended the military Conselho da Revolução and created the Tribunal Constitucional; later revisions followed, among other things, Portugal's membership of the European Union. A revision needs a two-thirds majority of the deputados.

The fundamental rights include equality before the law (artigo 13.º), the right to life (there is no death penalty in any case), freedom of expression, of religion and of association, and social rights such as health, education and housing.

Under the principle of equality, foreigners and stateless people living in Portugal have the same rights and duties as Portuguese citizens (artigo 15.º), with exceptions, especially for political rights and some public offices.

The Tribunal Constitucional has 13 judges: 10 are elected by the Assembleia da República and 3 are chosen by those judges. The Presidente da República can ask it to check a law before signing it, and courts can ask it to check a law in a concrete case.

Anyone can complain for free to the Provedor de Justiça (Ombudsman), who is elected by parliament, about unfair treatment or delays by public services, including immigration and tax services. The Provedor makes recommendations but does not judge.

topics.title: Unions, collective agreements and workers' rights
topics.sourceNote: Based on the Constitution (artigos 54.º–59.º), the Código do Trabalho and the information of the Autoridade para as Condições do Trabalho (act.gov.pt), as of 2026-11. Labour law changes often and your collective agreement may give you more rights; check your contract and the ACT. General orientation, not legal advice.
topics.intro: In Portugal workers' rights come from the Constitution, the Código do Trabalho and the collective agreement (convenção coletiva) of your sector. Unions, workers' commissions and the labour inspectorate ACT help to make these rights real at work.
topics.question: No teu país, os sindicatos têm muita força? (In your country, are trade unions strong?)
facts: The Constitution protects the freedom to join a union (sindicato), the right to strike and the right to elect a workers' commission. Nobody may be dismissed or treated worse for joining a union, and you do not have to tell your employer that you are a member.
The two large union confederations are the CGTP-IN and the UGT. Many unions are organised by sector or profession, such as teachers, nurses or transport workers.

A convenção coletiva is an agreement between unions and employers or employers' associations. It can set wages, working hours, holidays and other conditions above the legal minimum. The government can extend an agreement to the whole sector with a portaria de extensão, so it may apply to you even if you are not a union member.
In a company, workers can elect a comissão de trabalhadores, which has the right to be informed and consulted on important decisions, and unions can have delegados sindicais at the workplace.
A strike (greve) must be announced in advance with a pré-aviso. In essential services, such as hospitals and transport, minimum services (serviços mínimos) must be kept.

The Autoridade para as Condições do Trabalho (ACT) is the labour inspectorate. You can contact it with questions and file a complaint about problems such as unpaid wages, unsafe work or work without a contract. The ACT checks companies and can fine them.
